lessonTitle: Life-Cycle Assessment Method: Functional Unit, Inventory and Comparison

blocks.text: Two wheelbarrow tray designs are on the table: a pressed steel tray that is cheap and heavy, and a moulded polymer tray that is lighter but needs replacing sooner. Asking which has the lower footprint 'per tray' is the wrong question, because the trays do not last equally long. Life-cycle assessment (LCA) forces you to compare designs on the job they do, not on the object they are.

blocks.markdown: **Life-cycle assessment** is a standardised method (ISO 14040 and ISO 14044) for quantifying the environmental impact of a product across its life. It has four linked phases: **goal and scope definition**, **life-cycle inventory (LCI)**, **life-cycle impact assessment (LCIA)** and **interpretation**. The results of each phase can send you back to earlier ones.

rows: Why are we doing this, for whom, and what exactly is compared?
Functional unit, system boundary, assumptions, data quality
What goes in and out of each process?
Table of material, energy, transport and emissions flows
What do the flows mean for the environment?
Impact scores, such as global warming potential in kg CO2e
What do the results tell us, and how reliable are they?
blocks.caption: The four phases of LCA.

blocks.title: Functional unit
blocks.text: A quantified description of the function the product delivers, used as the common basis of comparison. It states what is delivered, how much, how well and for how long, for example: 'to carry 50 kg of load on this bracket for 20 years'.

blocks.markdown: The **system boundary** states which life-cycle stages and processes are included. **Cradle-to-gate** covers extraction to the factory gate; **cradle-to-grave** adds distribution, use and end of life; **cradle-to-cradle** closes the loop through reuse or recycling. A boundary must be the same for the designs being compared, and the decision to exclude a stage must be justified, for example because it is identical in both designs.

The inventory records, for each process in the boundary, the physical inputs (mass of materials, electricity in kWh, fuel, water, transport in tonne-km) and outputs (product, waste, emissions). Each flow is then multiplied by an **emission factor** from a database (typical values for steel, aluminium and electricity are tabulated in LCA databases and vary with region and recycled content) to give the impact.

blocks.caption: Embodied carbon of a part: m_i is the mass of material i (kg) with factor f_i (kg CO2e/kg); W_j is energy of type j (kWh) with grid factor g_j (kg CO2e/kWh).

blocks.title: Inventory and embodied carbon of two brackets
blocks.prompt: Bracket A is steel: 2.4 kg of steel at a typical 2.0 kg CO2e/kg plus 3.0 kWh of machining electricity. Bracket B is aluminium: 1.3 kg at a typical 9.0 kg CO2e/kg plus 4.5 kWh of electricity. Use a grid factor of 0.40 kg CO2e/kWh. Compute embodied carbon per bracket.
blocks.answer: Per bracket, A has 6.0 kg CO2e and B has 13.5 kg CO2e, so steel looks better per object. The functional unit may change this.

blocks.title: Changing the functional unit
blocks.prompt: Bracket A lasts 10 years in service and bracket B, being corrosion resistant, lasts 25 years. Compare them per year of service, assuming the same use-phase and end-of-life in both.

steps.text: Define the functional unit: one bracket supporting the load for one year. Embodied carbon is spread over the life.

Interpret: the aluminium bracket has lower impact per year of service, about 10% less, although it is higher per object. The result is sensitive to the assumed lives, so the interpretation phase should test them.

blocks.answer: On the basis of one bracket-year, aluminium (0.54) beats steel (0.60), reversing the per-object ranking.

blocks.caption: The choice of functional unit can change the ranking.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Comparing per kilogram or per item rather than per function; using different system boundaries for the two designs; mixing data of different ages or regions without saying so; and reporting a small difference as decisive without a sensitivity check.

blocks.title: Interpretation closes the loop
blocks.text: Report the result with its assumptions, test the sensitivity of the conclusion to the uncertain ones (life, recycled content, electricity factor) and say how large a difference must be before it matters.

points: LCA has four phases: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation.
The functional unit expresses the function delivered (amount, quality, duration) and the system boundary fixes which stages are counted; both must be identical for designs being compared.
The inventory lists material, energy and transport flows; multiplying by emission factors gives embodied carbon, and designs are compared per functional unit, not per object.

questions.stem: Two designs of centrifugal pump are to be compared by LCA. Which is the most suitable functional unit?

options.text: Delivery of 1000 cubic metres of water against a stated head over the service life
The purchase price of the pump

questions.correctOptionText: Delivery of 1000 cubic metres of water against a stated head over the service life

distractorRationale.a: Pumps differ in performance and life, so one pump is not the same function.
distractorRationale.b: Mass says nothing about the function.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it states the amount of service delivered, so designs of different size and life can be compared.
distractorRationale.d: Price is not a measure of function.

questions.explanation: A functional unit quantifies the service the product provides. For a pump this is the water delivered at a given head, which allows a fair comparison across different designs and lives.

questions.stem: A study compares two machine tool spindles whose use-phase electricity use dominates their impact and differs between the designs. Which system boundary is most appropriate?

distractorRationale.a: This would omit the stage that dominates and differs between designs.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the boundary must include the stage that drives the difference, namely use.
distractorRationale.c: Machining alone would ignore materials and use.
distractorRationale.d: Packaging is a minor and irrelevant stage here.

questions.explanation: The boundary should include any life stage that matters to the comparison. Excluding a dominant, unequal stage such as use would invalidate the conclusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following belongs to the life-cycle inventory phase rather than to another phase?

options.text: Recording the mass of aluminium ingot and the kWh of electricity used to cast a housing
Converting emissions into a global warming potential score

questions.correctOptionText: Recording the mass of aluminium ingot and the kWh of electricity used to cast a housing

distractorRationale.a: This is part of goal and scope.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: inventory records physical inputs and outputs of the processes.

questions.explanation: The inventory phase compiles quantified flows of materials, energy and emissions. Defining the unit, characterising the impact and making recommendations belong to the other phases.

questions.stem: A cast aluminium gearbox housing requires 4.5 kg of aluminium (typical embodied carbon 8.2 kg CO2e/kg), 12 kWh of machining electricity (grid factor 0.35 kg CO2e/kWh) and 0.8 kg of cutting fluid (1.1 kg CO2e/kg). Calculate the total embodied carbon of the housing in kg CO2e.
questions.explanation: Material: 4.5 x 8.2 = 36.9 kg CO2e. Electricity: 12 x 0.35 = 4.2 kg CO2e. Cutting fluid: 0.8 x 1.1 = 0.88 kg CO2e. The sum is 36.9 + 4.2 + 0.88 = 41.98, about 42.0 kg CO2e.

questions.stem: Design X of a conveyor idler has an embodied carbon of 42 kg CO2e and a service life of 8 years. Design Y has an embodied carbon of 60 kg CO2e and a service life of 15 years. Use-phase and end-of-life impacts are identical. By how much does X exceed Y in kg CO2e per year of service?
questions.explanation: Design X: 42/8 = 5.25 kg CO2e per year. Design Y: 60/15 = 4.00 kg CO2e per year. The difference is 5.25 - 4.00 = 1.25 kg CO2e per year, so the heavier-footprint design Y is actually better per unit of service.

questions.stem: For an LCA comparison, it is always valid to compare two designs per kilogram of finished product, because mass is an objective measure.
questions.explanation: A functional unit must describe the function delivered, not the mass of the product. Two designs may differ in mass, performance and life, so comparing per kilogram can reverse the correct ranking.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the four phases of an LCA according to ISO 14040/14044?

options.text: Inventory, goal and scope, impact assessment, interpretation
Goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment, interpretation
Impact assessment, inventory, goal and scope, interpretation
Goal and scope, impact assessment, inventory, interpretation

questions.correctOptionText: Goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment, interpretation

distractorRationale.a: The goal and scope must be set before inventory data are collected.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the framework runs from goal and scope to inventory, impact assessment and interpretation, with iteration.
distractorRationale.d: Impact assessment cannot precede the inventory.

questions.explanation: The logical order is to define the study, compile the flows, assess their impact, and interpret. Iteration between phases is allowed, but each phase depends on the earlier ones.

questions.stem: You are asked to compare a cast-iron and a polymer-composite design of a garden wheelbarrow tray by LCA. Define a suitable functional unit and system boundary, and justify any stage you exclude.
markingGuide: Functional unit states function, quantity and duration (for example carry a stated load in garden use for 10 years)
Recognises that designs with different lives must be compared on the same duration or per year of service
System boundary: cradle-to-grave or cradle-to-gate with use justified; states which stages are included (material production, manufacture, transport, use, end of life)
Exclusion is justified when the stage is identical in both designs or negligible, and is stated
questions.explanation: A good answer ties the functional unit to the function and duration, and treats the boundary as a stated, justified choice. Equal treatment of both designs is essential.

questions.stem: List the data you would need for a simple inventory of the embodied carbon of a stainless-steel pressure vessel, and explain how you would convert it to a carbon figure.
markingGuide: Material mass, including scrap and yield losses
Manufacturing energy by process (cutting, welding, forming) in kWh, with fuel
Transport distances and modes in tonne-km
Consumables such as welding wire and shielding gas
Emission factors from a database for each flow with units, matched to region and recycled content
Multiply each flow by its factor and sum to give kg CO2e; state data sources and assumptions
questions.explanation: The marker looks for physical flows with units and the use of emission factors to convert to carbon. Awareness of data quality and assumptions is expected.

questions.stem: Design P of a hydraulic power unit has an embodied carbon of 85 kg CO2e and a use-phase carbon of 12 kg CO2e per year. Design Q has an embodied carbon of 130 kg CO2e and a use-phase carbon of 7 kg CO2e per year. Both last 10 years with identical end-of-life. Compare them per functional unit of 10 years' service and discuss how confident you are in the result.
markingGuide: Total for P: 85 + 12 x 10 = 205 kg CO2e
Total for Q: 130 + 7 x 10 = 200 kg CO2e
Q is lower by 5 kg CO2e, about 2.4%
Notes the small margin relative to data uncertainty
Sensitivity: shorter life or different use would reverse the ranking (break-even life is 9 years: 45/5 = 9)
Recommends checking assumptions and uncertainty before concluding
questions.explanation: Calculating the totals correctly is the first step, but the discussion of the small 2.4% margin and the break-even life is what earns the higher marks. Interpretation should always include a sensitivity check.
